newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels making headway on deal - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels making headway on deal - diplomats.

text.p: Peruvian hostage-takers would take up asylum in Cuba and might take some of their 72 captives with them under a draft agreement to end the standoff at the Japanese ambassador's home, diplomats said on Tuesday.

Other parts of the deal have yet to be negotiated, a process that could take a couple of weeks, the diplomats said. But for the first time in the 98-day standoff momentum was building toward a deal to free the hostages and let their captors take up a Caribbean exile, they said.

"There really is a certain degree of optimism," Bolivia's acting ambassador, Eloy Avila, told local Radio Programas. "We see flexibility on the part of the government and the MRTA," he said. Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio is one of the hostages.

The main obstacle now is the demand by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels for freedom for hundreds of jailed comrades -- a demand rejected by President Alberto Fujimori, diplomatic sources said.
"Asylum seems to be pretty well sewn up," said one diplomat. "The core issue now is what to do about the prisoners. That's the real area of contention."

Cuba and the Dominican Republic have offered asylum as long as it forms part of an overall settlement to the siege, in which 72 men are being held by the rebels in a house with no electricity or running water. The rebels initially spurned asylum, saying they preferred to return to armed struggle after winning release of their comrades, but have since said they could accept asylum for at least some of their number.
"There has been much progress on the asylum issue and the talks have moved on to other issues," one diplomat said.

"For a long time the talks seemed to be going up and down every day. But now there's progress, there's a mood of optimism," another said, cautioning that even if talks went smoothly from now on freedom for hostages could be 10 days to two weeks away.

The guerrillas could take some of the hostages with them on their Cubana de Aviacion flight to guarantee safe passage, a Japanese diplomat said. The government initially rejected that rebel demand but later agreed to let the rebels take at least eight hostages, including Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and Japanese Ambassador Morihisha Aoki, the source added.

The MRTA rebels took more than 500 guests hostage on Dec. 17 after blasting into a gala cocktail party at the ambassador's residence. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping an array of Cabinet ministers, ambassadors and Japanese businessmen with which to bargain with Fujimori.
Asylum is part of the draft deal hammered out by a three-man mediation team after talks with both sides, sources said.

After a break for Holy Week, in which mediator and Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani will leave Lima to lead religious festivities in his diocese of Ayacucho, the mediators will meet again with the MRTA early next week, a diplomat said.
In the latest of a flurry of meetings, Canadian Ambassador and mediator Anthony Vincent met the MRTA command inside the residence on Tuesday.

"All this does not mean we are at the doorstep of a solution but it does mean we have reached a road that will take us to a solution," Avila said. "We hope that with the next conversations starting on Monday or Tuesday we will have something to celebrate."

News reports have said the final agreement could also include improvements in prison conditions for MRTA inmates and payment of a multimillion dollar ransom to the group, but diplomats said they were unsure about the last point.

Avila said the thorny issue of the MRTA's demand for freedom for its jailed comrades could be settled by granting pardons to some prisoners accused of non-violent crimes. He said some cases were already being examined by a Peruvian government panel looking into cases of people falsely imprisoned on terrorism charges without due process.

"They wouldn't be freed but rather granted a pardon in accordance with (the recommendations of) a commission that already exists in Peru and with respect to some people who did not commit violent crimes," he said.
There was no chance of an outright release of convicted MRTA guerrillas, one diplomat said.
